chapters.title: Chapter 2: How Trade Wars Move Markets

lessons.title: FII Flows and the Nifty: How Indian Markets Reacted to Past Trade War Episodes

children.text: You now know the three channels a trade war travels through. This lesson looks at what actually happened when those channels fired, across three real episodes, and at one especially useful case that teaches you how to tell a trade-war-driven selloff apart from a purely domestic one.

body.caption: Trade War Stress Episodes and How Indian Markets Responded

cells: IL&FS default, trade war escalation, and a crude oil price spike, hitting together
Sharp correction from the August 2018 peak into October
Stabilized into early 2019 as oil prices eased and IL&FS-linked NBFC stress was contained
Yuan crossed 7/USD, US-China tariffs escalated further, compounded by a domestic FPI surcharge from India's own July 2019 budget
Sharp fall through most of August
Heavy net selling, both global and domestically triggered
Partial reversal after India rolled back the surcharge and announced corporate tax cuts in September 2019
US tariffs on India (25%, then 50%) tied to Russian oil purchases
Export-heavy sectors underperformed; broader index reaction more contained and sector-specific than 2018
Volatile, mixed flows through the year rather than one sustained wave
Ongoing at the time of writing

children.text: The Clean Case: Domestic vs. Global, August 2019

markDefs.definition: An additional tax India's July 2019 budget imposed on individuals and certain trust-structured entities above a high income threshold. Many FPIs were structured as trusts and got caught by it, which triggered domestic-specific selling that had nothing to do with the trade war happening on the other side of the world at the same time.

children.text: August 2019 is the single best teaching example in this course, because two shocks landed at once and you can actually tell them apart. Globally, the yuan had just broken past 7 per dollar and the US-China trade war was escalating further. Domestically, India's July 2019 budget had imposed an

that unexpectedly hit many FPIs structured as trusts, triggering FII selling that had nothing to do with China or the yuan. Both stories were true simultaneously, and most headlines at the time blurred them into one "trade war hits markets" narrative.

body.label: Corporate Tax Cut Announcement
body.context: India cut its base corporate tax rate to 22% (15% for new manufacturing companies), sparking one of the sharpest single-day Nifty and Sensex rallies in years, even though the global trade war was still very much escalating at the time

body.text: That rally is the tell. If a purely domestic policy reversal, a tax cut with nothing to do with China or the US, can spark that sharp a recovery while the global trade war is still running hot, then the preceding selloff was never a pure trade war story. Part of it was India's own surcharge decision, and undoing that domestic decision undid a large part of the damage.

children.text: Look across all three episodes and a few things repeat. FII/FPI selling acts as an amplifier, not usually the sole cause, it makes an existing move sharper and faster rather than starting one from nothing. Domestic institutional buying has grown more capable of cushioning the fall each time, which is part of why 2025's reaction looked more contained and sector-specific than 2018's broad correction. India VIX spikes early and tends to fade faster than the underlying index recovers. And defensive sectors, FMCG, utilities, pharma where it is not directly tariffed, hold up better than export-heavy, high-beta names in the first leg of every episode.

body.title: Signs You're in a Trade-War-Driven Selloff, Not Something Else
steps: Check whether a domestic-only catalyst (a budget provision, an RBI policy shift, a local credit event) is also live at the same time, the way the FPI surcharge was in August 2019
Check if the selloff is broad-based across sectors (more consistent with a global shock) or concentrated in export-heavy names (more consistent with a trade-specific one)
Check whether other emerging markets are falling on the same days for the same reason, a genuinely global trade war shock rarely hits India alone
Watch what actually ends the selloff: a global trade de-escalation headline points to trade war as the real driver, a purely domestic policy reversal points to a domestic driver instead

body.title: Know the Number
body.prompt: In September 2019, India cut its base corporate tax rate to what percentage?
body.explanation: The base corporate tax rate was cut to 22% (effectively about 25.17% including surcharge and cess), with an even lower 15% rate offered to new manufacturing companies, announced on September 20, 2019.

body.text: Every real market selloff blamed on a trade war usually has at least one domestic thread running through it too. Learning to separate the two is what turns "the market fell because of tariffs" from a headline into an actual, testable claim.

points: Three episodes, Sep-Oct 2018, Aug 2019, and 2025, show the same basic shape: FII/FPI selling amplifies an existing shock, and the reaction has gotten more sector-specific and less broad-based over time as DII buying has grown.

August 2019 is the clearest teaching case: a global trade war shock (yuan past 7) and a domestic policy shock (the FPI surcharge) hit at the same time, and only one of them was undone by India's September 2019 corporate tax cut, yet markets rallied sharply anyway.
That mismatch, a domestic-only fix producing a sharp recovery during an still-escalating global trade war, is the actual evidence that the August 2019 selloff was not purely a trade war story.

A practical checklist beats a headline: check for concurrent domestic catalysts, check whether the move is broad-based or sector-specific, check whether other emerging markets are moving too, and watch what actually ends the selloff.
